extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, translators, and literary scholars (writers studying Aristotle's Poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating epic and tragic poetry (diction, plot structure, verisimilitude, theatricality, and errors of imitation) based on Aristotle's Poetics. Focuses on unity of action, appropriate diction, use of episodes, and how to handle plausibility and faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single integrated action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem (whether dramatic or narrative) should be organized around one action so that its parts tend to one end; the whole should present 'one animal' to the spectator, producing a single, complete pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct episodes and characters so that each contributes to the single plotline; avoid grouping unrelated events or distinct stories that prevent a single unified end. Unity of action is essential for tragic effect and should be pursued in epic too (by making each episode cohere toward the whole). Examples: tragedies staged around one action; epics may be larger but should still preserve unity within their parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integrated part of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus is counted as one and should be a part of the whole fable, not an extraneous addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the chorus so its role advances or complements the action rather than interrupting it; the chorus should aim toward the same end as the plot and be harmonized with the dramatic movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include peripeteia, recognition, passions, sententia, and elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic works require the same formal elements as tragedy: reversals (peripeteia), recognitions (agnitio), the stirring of passions, well-turned sententiae (maxims/phrases), and fitting elocution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure key dramatic moments (reversal/recognition) are present and that the language and moral sentiments align with the emotional effects intended (pity, fear, etc.). These are needed in epic as in tragedy to produce the required effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expository 'histories' in place of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems that merely recount events (histories) without being unified actions fail the proper imitation and should be avoided when the aim is dramatic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor enacted or vividly represented actions that create unity over mere narration of successive unrelated events; if using episodes, bind them so that each incident relates causally or thematically to the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic verisimilitude (choose plausible seeming events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer events that, though perhaps beyond strict probability, appear believable to the audience (verisimile) rather than merely possible events that are poorly fitted to persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select incidents and causal chains that the audience can accept as credible in context; impossible-but-plausible choices are often more effective rhetorically than merely possible-but-unconvincing ones. Use aesthetic devices to make the implausible acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid including things 'without reason' (ratione vacua)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce elements that lack rationale or justification; gratuitous, irrational facts harm the poem unless later rendered coherent by the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an initially implausible or unjustified detail is inserted, ensure subsequent parts of the work reconcile it; otherwise remove or alter it. Occasional prefiguring that later becomes coherent may excuse earlier implausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elocution should be perspicuous and dignified
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of poetic diction is clarity (perspicua) without being lowly (nec humilis tamen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that is clear to the audience but maintains appropriate dignity for the genre and subject. Avoid overly low or common diction when it undercuts the poem's seriousness, and avoid obscurity that hides character or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid barbarisms and enigmatic mixed-language constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not slip into barbarisms (incorrect foreignisms) or produce aenigmata (riddling, mixed-out-of-place expressions) that confuse rather than elucidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not indiscriminately mix foreign forms or translations into the diction; such occurrences are 'barbarisms' and make the speech unintelligible or awkward. If using foreign or transferred terms, ensure they are intelligible and serve a purpose (e.g., grandeur) rather than creating confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proper, vernacular, translated, and ornamented names appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and vocabulary may be proper (native), vernacular, translated, ornamented, made, prolonged, or contracted; select the type of name that suits the metre, genre, and intended effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match names and lexicon to the metric and stylistic needs: heroic (epic) meter allows more varied/learned vocabulary, iambic favors colloquial words. Transposing names across languages or inventing words is permissible but should be used sparingly and only when the poet has the skill to make them fit and be intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transference and coinage as marks of talent (use cautiously)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating new words or transferring foreign words into one’s language is permitted but is a sign of acute talent and requires natural aptitude and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only attempt novel coinages or daring translations if you can make them seem natural in context and useful to the poem; poorly handled neologisms or calques are objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction and vocabulary to meter and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different meters and genres require different wordstocks: heroic (epic) allows learned/vulgar/transferred names; iambic imitates everyday speech and thus uses familiar words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose lexicon consistent with the rhetorical and metrical character: epic (heroic) diction tolerates lofty or foreign terms; iambic/dramatic speech should sound like spoken colloquial language where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elocution should repair weak parts; avoid ornament that obscures character
rubrics_metrics.description: Elocution must work hardest in parts of the fable that lack strong moral action or sententiae (the 'ignavis' parts), but excessive splendor in style that obscures moral traits or thought is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stylistic ornamentation to strengthen weak narrative stretches, but not to mask poor characterization or to hide a lack of thought. Balance ornament with clarity and character revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of false reasoning/paralogisms as a poetic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may employ fallacious-seeming deductions (paralogisms) or 'false reasons' that appear convincing to the audience and thereby create wonder; rhetorical plausibility can trump formal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such devices only when they generate admiration or persuasive effect; prefer fallacies that the audience will accept as true rather than formally valid arguments that fail to move or convince. Be cautious: overuse or crude fallacy can embarrass the poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and seriousness of poetic errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic error is of two kinds—errors 'per se' (intrinsic to the poet/poem) and errors 'per accidens' (borrowed or accidental); critics reproach poets on five grounds: things impossible, things lacking reason, pernicious/improper things, contradictions (subcontraria), and deviations from the poetic/artistic norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or revising a poem, diagnose which category of reproach applies and address it by reference to the relevant formal differences. Some errors are more culpable (intrinsic) than others (accidental); consider whether the poet deliberately chose departures for effect and whether they can be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: When imitation is blameworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: If imitation depicts things impossible in themselves (intrinsically impossible) it is a substantive error; if the poet invents things that 'ought to be' or that are believed by the people, those are treated differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the poet on whether the imitation aims at what 'is', 'was', 'is thought to be', or 'ought to be'; only some departures are permissible as poetic devices. If the poem invents intrinsically impossible acts without artistic justification, it's a clear fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate theatricality and restraint in gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should not rely on excessive on-stage motion or gesticulation; such theatrical burdens (onerous motion) belong more to the histrionic than to poetic art and can be detrimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale physical action and stagecraft to the decorum of the genre; avoid over-gesticulation that distracts from imitation or that was merely a histrionic habit. Tragedy may be presented without lavish motion and still be effective; do not let spectacle substitute for poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose medium appropriate to scope: epic vs. tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide between epic and tragedy based on what best achieves imitation's ends: tragedy is typically superior when the imitation can be concentrated into a single unified, intense action; epic offers magnitude and variety but risks dilution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story's unity, emotional intensity, and swiftly achieving of the poetic end are best served by concentrated action, prefer tragedy; if breadth, multiplicity of episodes, and extended narrative are required and can be handled without losing unity, epic may be appropriate. Consider audience, length, and the medium's capacity to produce pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narration and episodic structure to maintain variety without losing unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic can employ multiple episodes and parts to increase magnitude and variety, but each episode should still contribute to the overall unity and not create an incoherent multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize episodes so that individual episodes could, in some sense, be seen as cohesive units while remaining subordinate to the poem's single end. Avoid assembling many independent fables that do not integrate into one imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization must be justifiable and motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' actions and moral qualities must be plausible given their nature; culpable faults include portraying persons as acting immorally without cause (improbitas) or leaving motives unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always supply motives, context, or lawful reasons for characters' morally questionable acts; where a poet attributes vice or error to a character, make it intelligible in terms of their disposition, circumstances, or higher reasons (e.g., greater good, necessity). Unmotivated depravity invites reproach.
